title: Spiral Galaxy NGC 4395
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 4395, imaged by the Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage) and H. Schweiker (WIYN and NOIRLab/NSF/AURA)

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: NGC 4395, in the constellation Canes Venatici, is a spiral whose surface brightness is very low, meaning its light is spread thinly across its disc. Unlike most galaxies, its centre is small and faint rather than a bright, concentrated bulge.

Almost every galaxy is known to hold a supermassive black hole at its heart, and NGC 4395 is no exception. But its black hole is one of the smallest of its kind yet found, six times smaller than the one at the centre of our own Milky Way.

Small central black holes like this interest astronomers because they may help show how such objects grow and how they relate to the galaxies around them. A faint, diffuse galaxy with a modest core offers a very different case from the big, bright spirals that are more commonly studied.

understand.summary: The Mosaic camera on the Mayall 4-meter Telescope used four filters. B is shown in blue, V in green, I in orange and hydrogen-alpha in red.

understand.eye: A galaxy this faint and diffuse would be almost impossible to see by eye; long exposures on a large telescope bring out its disc.
